content:
Hello Corvale Mobility team,

I’m applying for the Cloud Infrastructure / DevOps Contractor – Fleet Connectivity role. I’m a QA automation engineer looking to move into infrastructure engineering full time, and your work connecting a new train fleet to cloud services is an opportunity to apply the CI/CD and infrastructure experience I’ve built across three product teams.

At Odrava Health Software, I own GitLab CI pipelines for approximately 25 developers. By parallelising test jobs, caching dependencies and separating end-to-end tests, I reduced average pipeline time from 38 to 14 minutes and monthly runner costs by approximately 30%. I also built short-lived merge-request environments with Docker Compose and later Helm on a shared Kubernetes cluster. These give teams an environment to review changes and run tests before merging; the platform team operates the cluster.

Alongside this work, I built a personal k3s cluster using Argo CD for GitOps, Prometheus, Grafana and Loki for monitoring, and cert-manager for TLS. I also used Terraform to provision a personal Hetzner VPS and am learning the basics of AWS EC2 and S3. I’ve written CI documentation used for onboarding and built Grafana dashboards that helped teams identify flaky tests and reduce their rate from 7% to below 1%.

What appeals to me about this role is the chance to help shape infrastructure that is secure, observable and practical for developers to operate. I would welcome the opportunity to discuss how my experience in test infrastructure and my personal projects could contribute to Corvale’s fleet connectivity team.

Thank you for your time and consideration.

Marta Kowal-Brandt
marta.kowalbrandt@example.com | +48 555 303 303 | gitlab.com/mkb-example

critique.content_quality_feedback: The cover letter is clear, professional, and factually consistent with the candidate information. It uses strong quantified evidence: pipeline time reduced from 38 to 14 minutes, runner costs reduced by approximately 30%, and flaky tests reduced from 7% to below 1%. The letter also explains the transition from QA automation into infrastructure engineering without overstating production Kubernetes or cloud ownership. However, it is somewhat defensive and underdeveloped for a contractor role involving architecture, stakeholder engagement, secure connectivity, and end-to-production ownership. The opening focuses on wanting to move into infrastructure rather than leading with the infrastructure work already performed. The letter also omits relevant evidence from the candidate material, including documentation used for onboarding, mentoring two interns, and collaboration with QA and product teams around merge-request environments.
critique.ats_compatibility_feedback: The document is ATS-friendly in plain text: it has a standard greeting, readable paragraphs, no tables or graphics, and relevant searchable terms including GitLab CI, Docker Compose, Helm, Kubernetes, k3s, Argo CD, Prometheus, Grafana, Loki, cert-manager, TLS, Terraform, AWS EC2, and S3. Keyword coverage is nevertheless limited for this particular role. The letter does not mention systems architecture, system design, networking, security awareness, stakeholder engagement, technical leadership, or Terragrunt. Some of these are genuine candidate gaps rather than wording defects, so they should not be added without evidence. The document could also improve ATS and recruiter relevance by explicitly describing the merge-request environments as infrastructure that supports application deployment, observability, testing, and developer operation.
critique.job_alignment_feedback: The strongest alignment is with hands-on infrastructure engineering around CI/CD, ephemeral environments, Kubernetes deployments, monitoring, TLS certificate management, Terraform-based personal infrastructure, analytical improvement, and clear technical documentation. The quantified pipeline and reliability outcomes are particularly persuasive. The candidate also has some relevant AWS exposure through EC2 and S3 learning, but not professional AWS operation. The main role gaps are strong Terraform and Terragrunt, production cloud environment design and operation, systems architecture and system design, mTLS, practical security work, IoT or remote-device integration, and demonstrated technical leadership with external stakeholders such as train manufacturers. The candidate's material also does not show virtual-machine experience or backend/full-stack development beyond Java test code. These are capability gaps, not defects in the cover letter. Cultural alignment is present only indirectly through references to practical infrastructure and helping developers; the letter does not strongly connect the candidate's experience to Corvale's emphasis on ownership, collaborative problem-solving, and end-to-end system operation.
critique.improvement_instructions:
CRITICAL / HIGH-VALUE IMPROVEMENTS:
1. In the opening paragraph, replace the sentence "I’m a QA automation engineer looking to move into infrastructure engineering full time" with a more evidence-led statement that does not foreground the career gap. For example: "My experience combines CI/CD ownership, ephemeral Kubernetes environments, infrastructure tooling, and observability across three product teams, and I am now applying that foundation to a dedicated infrastructure engineering role." This remains truthful while presenting the candidate's existing infrastructure work more strongly.

2. In the second paragraph, make the scope of the merge-request environment work more explicit by changing "I also built short-lived merge-request environments with Docker Compose and later Helm on a shared Kubernetes cluster" to: "I built short-lived merge-request environments containing the application, PostgreSQL, and seeded test data, first with Docker Compose and later with Helm on a shared Kubernetes cluster; the environments were created from GitLab CI and automatically removed after merge or 48 hours of inactivity." This adds supported implementation detail and better matches the job's infrastructure build-and-operation language.

3. In the paragraph describing collaboration, add the supported stakeholder and communication evidence after the merge-request environment sentence: "These environments gave QA and product colleagues a place to review changes and run end-to-end tests before merging. I also wrote internal CI documentation used in onboarding and mentored two QA interns." This strengthens alignment with stakeholder engagement, clear communication, and bringing others along without claiming formal technical leadership.

4. In the final paragraph, replace the generic sentence "What appeals to me about this role is the chance to help shape infrastructure that is secure, observable and practical for developers to operate" with a more concrete, evidence-based version: "What appeals to me about this role is the opportunity to help shape infrastructure that is observable and practical for developers to operate—an approach I have applied through ephemeral environments, CI-result dashboards, and tooling that improved pipeline speed and test reliability." Do not describe the candidate as having designed secure train-to-cloud communication, mTLS, or production fleet infrastructure, because those experiences are not supported.

5. In the final paragraph, connect the candidate's experience to Corvale's collaborative ownership model without inventing company-specific experience. For example, add: "I would value contributing to a team that owns systems end to end and solves infrastructure problems collaboratively." This is a truthful response to the culture information and is more specific than the current generic closing.

MINOR ATS / PRESENTATION ENHANCEMENT:
6. In the paragraph about personal infrastructure, retain "Terraform" and "TLS" exactly as written and add the supported networking term "Traefik ingress": "I also used Terraform to provision a personal Hetzner VPS and configured Traefik ingress and cert-manager for TLS in the homelab." Do not add Terragrunt or mTLS, since the candidate information does not support either tool or capability.
